notes: Adversarial path on an explicitly named prospective observational study. Seven fixture records are retrieved. A discovery reply appends three model leads after them (D1); the first lead gives its year as the boolean true, which is refused (stored null, invalid-type at items[0].year). inputs.need:
I am a colorectal surgeon and co-chair of the surgical site infection working group at a 600-bed teaching hospital. We do about 380 colorectal resections a year, elective and emergency. Our infection prevention team's active 30-day surveillance found a surgical site infection after 14 percent of resections last year, which is higher than the regional average. Two years ago we adopted a seven-element bundle: oral antibiotics with mechanical bowel preparation for elective cases, chlorhexidine-alcohol skin preparation, antibiotic prophylaxis within 60 minutes before incision, normothermia, glucose below 11 mmol/L, a wound protector, and a glove and instrument change before closure. Nobody knows how reliably each element is delivered, and the working group keeps arguing about which elements matter.

We plan a prospective observational study: for every colorectal resection, theatre staff would record each bundle element on a short form, and the surveillance nurses would follow patients for 30 days, including after discharge by phone. We want to know how often each element and the full bundle are delivered, and whether full bundle compliance is associated with fewer infections after accounting for emergency surgery, stoma formation, diabetes, obesity and operation length.

I need help with the compliance form, how to define full compliance when some elements do not apply (bowel preparation in emergency cases), the sample size and whether one year is enough, the analysis of the association without overclaiming causation, and how to keep post-discharge follow-up complete. Our infection prevention team already does surveillance, and the hospital's quality council has approved the data collection.
inputs.constraints: No new funding. The compliance form must take under two minutes in theatre. Surveillance nurses can make one follow-up call per patient at day 30.

records.title: Care bundle compliance and surgical site infection after colorectal resection: a prospective multicentre study
records.authors: Achebe-Sandoval R, Lindqvist-Mwangi P, Okonkwo-Hartley J
records.abstract: In 2,140 colorectal resections across 11 hospitals, full compliance with a six-element bundle was recorded in 38 percent. Surgical site infection occurred in 9.8 percent of fully compliant cases and 16.1 percent of others (adjusted odds ratio 0.61, 95 percent CI 0.46 to 0.81). Oral antibiotic bowel preparation and wound protectors showed the strongest individual associations. Infection was ascertained by active surveillance until day 30, including a telephone review after discharge. Compliance was recorded by theatre staff who knew the study aim, and emergency cases were fewer than a fifth of the sample.

records.title: Which bundle elements matter? An element-level analysis in elective colorectal surgery
records.abstract: Using data on 860 elective colorectal resections, we examined each of seven bundle elements. Oral antibiotic prophylaxis with bowel preparation was associated with lower infection (odds ratio 0.52), while glove change before closure showed no clear association. Elements were strongly correlated with each other, so individual estimates are unstable and should not be used to drop elements. Emergency cases were excluded, and compliance was taken from the operation note rather than recorded at the time. The authors call for prospective recording of each element at the time of surgery.

records.title: Surgical site infection bundles in colorectal surgery: a systematic review and meta-analysis
records.authors: Castellanos-Fairweather L, Oyelowo-Brandt E, Sato-Nilsen K, Reid-Achterberg D
records.abstract: Across 24 studies, most of them before-and-after comparisons, bundles were associated with lower surgical site infection after colorectal surgery (risk ratio 0.56, 95 percent CI 0.46 to 0.68). Studies with higher compliance reported larger reductions. Heterogeneity was high and bundle contents varied from 4 to 12 elements. Only 5 studies included post-discharge surveillance, so infections diagnosed after discharge were probably missed in most studies. Bundles that included oral antibiotic preparation reported the largest reductions, and publication bias was likely because small studies without an effect were rarely reported.

records.title: Post-discharge surveillance and missed surgical site infections after colorectal surgery
records.abstract: Of 412 surgical site infections detected after colorectal resection in three hospitals, 47 percent were diagnosed after discharge. A telephone call at day 30 by a surveillance nurse detected 83 percent of the post-discharge infections found by a combined clinic and telephone approach. Patients who could not be reached by phone were older and more often lived alone. Without post-discharge surveillance, infection rates would have been underestimated by almost half. Infections found after discharge were more often superficial but still led to unplanned clinic visits and readmissions.

records.title: Defining compliance when bundle elements do not apply: all-or-none measurement with applicability rules
records.abstract: We compared ways of scoring full bundle compliance when some elements do not apply. Counting non-applicable elements as delivered inflated full compliance in emergency cases from 31 to 44 percent, while excluding cases with any non-applicable element removed most emergency cases. An all-or-none score over applicable elements, with written applicability rules agreed in advance, gave stable estimates and could be completed in under two minutes on a paper form. Agreement between two independent scorers was high when the applicability rules were written down in advance.

records.title: Emergency colorectal surgery and surgical site infection: contamination, stoma formation and bundle delivery
records.authors: Varga-Nwosu B, Kimura-Lindgren A, Brennan-Mbeki O
records.abstract: In 1,030 emergency colorectal resections, surgical site infection occurred in 21 percent. Faecal contamination (odds ratio 2.4) and stoma formation were the strongest predictors. Full bundle compliance was recorded in only 19 percent of emergency cases, mainly because normothermia and glucose control were not documented. The authors warn that comparing compliant and non-compliant cases without adjusting for emergency status and contamination will exaggerate any bundle effect. Wound protectors were used in only half of emergency cases, and infection rates were similar across surgeons once contamination and stoma formation were taken into account.

records.title: Normothermia and glucose control during colorectal surgery: measurement from anaesthesia records
records.abstract: Reviewing 600 anaesthesia records for colorectal resections, we found an end-of-surgery temperature below 36.0 degrees in 18 percent of patients and no glucose measurement in 41 percent of patients without diabetes. Electronic anaesthesia records captured temperature reliably, but glucose values were often recorded only on paper charts. The authors recommend recording both elements at the end of surgery on the bundle form rather than extracting them later from anaesthesia records. Hypothermia was more common in operations lasting more than three hours and in patients over 80.

response.synthesis: Seven retrieved records, appraised at abstract level. A multicentre prospective study associated full bundle compliance with fewer infections (adjusted odds ratio 0.61), and a meta-analysis of mostly before-and-after studies agrees, while element-level estimates are unstable because elements are correlated. Almost half of infections appear after discharge, and a day-30 call finds most of them. Compliance must be scored over applicable elements, and emergency surgery, with low compliance and high infection, confounds the comparison. Three model leads remain unverified.
response.gradeRationale: Observational and before-and-after evidence with confounding by emergency status and unblinded compliance recording; consistent direction, low certainty for a causal effect.

response.reading: Infection follows from patient risk (emergency surgery, contamination, stoma, diabetes, obesity), from operation length and from which bundle elements were actually delivered. Emergency cases have both more infection and less compliance, so an unadjusted comparison would credit the bundle with the difference between emergency and elective surgery. Elements travel together, so element-level estimates are unstable. Half of the outcome happens after discharge, and patients living alone are the hardest to reach.

store.title: Surgical site infection bundle compliance after colorectal resection: a prospective observational study

response.overview: Prospective observational study of all colorectal resections from January 2027 to December 2028, recording bundle elements on a two-minute form in theatre and surgical site infection by active 30-day surveillance with a day-30 phone call.
response.population: All adults having elective or emergency colorectal resection at the hospital; no exclusions except patients who die within 48 hours.
response.exposure: Full compliance: every applicable bundle element delivered, scored all-or-none over applicable elements using written applicability rules (for example, bowel preparation does not apply to emergency cases). Element-level delivery is recorded for description.
response.procedures: The circulating nurse and anaesthetist complete the form at the end of surgery, including end-of-surgery temperature and the latest glucose. Surveillance nurses review inpatients and call every patient at day 30, with up to three attempts and a clinic check for those not reached. Covariates (emergency status, contamination class, stoma, diabetes, body mass index 35 or more, operation over 180 minutes) come from the operation note.

response.designSummary: Prospective observational study; logistic regression of 30-day infection on full compliance with six covariates.
response.sampleSize: About 380 resections a year with 14 percent infection give about 53 infections a year. If 40 percent of cases are fully compliant and the true adjusted odds ratio is near 0.6, one year gives about 50 percent power at two-sided alpha 0.05; 24 months (about 760 resections and 106 infections) gives about 77 percent power and about 18 events per covariate. The 12-month report is descriptive only.
response.primaryAnalysis: Logistic regression of infection within 30 days on full compliance, adjusted for emergency status, contamination class, stoma formation, diabetes, body mass index 35 or more and operation over 180 minutes; results also shown separately for elective and emergency cases.
response.secondaryAnalysis: Element-level compliance described without element-level effect estimates; deep or organ-space infection; sensitivity analysis counting unreached patients as infected and as not infected.
response.missingData: Missing covariates handled by multiple imputation with 20 imputations; patients not reached after three attempts and a clinic check are reported and bounded in the sensitivity analysis.
response.multiplicity: One primary association; secondary outcomes with confidence intervals only.
response.software: R; analysis plan fixed before the first form is completed.
response.summary: Twenty-four months give about 77 percent power for an odds ratio near 0.6; one year would give about 50 percent.

response.risks: Minimal: recording care already given and an existing follow-up call.
response.consent: Exempt as quality assurance with publication permitted (REB-EX-26-311); patients are informed through the pre-operative leaflet and may decline the use of their data for publication.
response.data: Forms hold a study number; linkage to surveillance is by the infection prevention team; reports never identify individual surgeons or theatre staff.
response.equity: PROGRESS-Plus: older patients, people living alone, people with limited English and people without a phone are most likely to be missed by the day-30 call, and emergency patients receive fewer elements. Interpreters are used for calls, a clinic check replaces unanswered calls, and results are reported for emergency and elective cases and by age.
response.effectiveness: Shows where the bundle fails and whether full delivery goes with fewer infections.
response.efficiency: Existing surveillance plus two minutes per operation.
response.partnerships: Infection prevention, theatre nursing, anaesthesia, two patient partners who had wound infections, and the regional surgical quality network.
response.rebPath: REB exemption as quality assurance with publication permitted (REB-EX-26-311); ICH-GCP and Declaration of Helsinki principles for confidentiality.
response.limitations: Observational; residual confounding; recording may change practice.
response.summary: Minimal-risk study under an REB exemption with attention to patients hard to reach after discharge.

response.partnershipPlan: Two patient partners who had wound infections review the day-30 call script and the results summary.
response.socialListening: No social media listening; complaints mentioning wound problems from the last two years are read for themes.

response.title: Bundle compliance and surgical site infection after colorectal resection: a prospective observational study with post-discharge surveillance
response.abstract: Objective: to measure element-level and full bundle compliance and estimate the association of full compliance with 30-day surgical site infection. Design: prospective observational study of all colorectal resections over 24 months. Results will be written after data collection.
response.introduction: Bundles are associated with fewer infections after colorectal surgery in mostly uncontrolled studies. Local delivery of each element and its association with infection, including infections after discharge, are unknown.
response.methods: Theatre staff recorded each element on a two-minute form, and full compliance was scored all-or-none over applicable elements. Surveillance nurses followed every patient for 30 days with a day-30 call, and logistic regression adjusted for six pre-specified covariates.
response.results: No data have been collected yet. The report will present element-level and full compliance for elective and emergency cases, infection rates and the adjusted association.
response.discussion: The discussion will interpret the association as an association and note that the cited multicentre record failed an identity check and must be re-appraised. It will consider recording effects and confounding by emergency status.
response.limitations: The design is observational and confounded by emergency status. Recording may itself change practice.
response.conclusion: To be written after analysis. It will describe compliance and an adjusted association, not the effect of individual elements.
